opening.headline: This explains why some requests fail during rolling updates by examining the speed and order in which deployments change pods.
body: During the deployment of a new version, error responses may temporarily increase. This occurs because the old pods have already been terminated, but the new pods have not yet become ready to receive requests. This gap becomes longer in AI services that take a long time to load models.

In this lesson, we examine how deployments replace pods through ReplicaSets, how to control the replacement speed using maxSurge and maxUnavailable, and how to roll back when issues occur. Finally, we'll configure settings together for a service with long model loading times.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the operation of rolling updates and rollbacks
The effects of maxSurge and maxUnavailable on availability can be distinguished.

screens.title: Some requests fail during rolling updates
screens.lead: There are three symptoms that may occur during deployment. When you select any of these symptoms, considerations will be displayed.

visual.alt: Scenario where some requests fail during deployment, as old pods are being terminated and new pods are not yet ready.

items.prompt: Error responses temporarily increase during the deployment of a new version.
items.answer: During deployment, both old and new pods coexist, and the pod count continues to change. In this phase, if there are insufficient pods available to handle actual requests, errors increase.

items.prompt: The old pod is gone, but a new pod has yet to be ready to receive requests.
items.answer: The fact that a pod has been created is different from the fact that it is ready to receive requests. If old pods are reduced before new pods are ready, service capacity will be temporarily degraded.

items.prompt: A method is needed to roll back to a previous version when an issue occurs.
items.answer: If a new version is unstable, it should be possible to quickly roll back to a previous state. Deployment records the previous revision and provides a rollback feature.

screens.outro: The question for this class is this: How does deployment change pods in terms of speed and order?

screens.title: Preview: Deployment Failure
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: Have you experienced outages during deployment?
items.answer: Deployment failures are often due to issues with the rollout process rather than code problems. The new version itself is normal, but the sequence and speed of the rollout temporarily reduce service capacity.

items.prompt: At that time, how many instances of the new version and the old version were running simultaneously?
items.answer: Setting this value is exactly what maxSurge and maxUnavailable are about. By knowing the default values and how the available pod count changes from those values, you can calculate and verify the cause of outages.

items.prompt: When rolling back, what was used as the basis to determine the previous state?
items.answer: During deployment, a new revision is created each time the pod template changes, and the target for rollback is specified as a revision. When the baseline is clearly defined, the rollback operation can be completed with a single command.

screens.outro: First, let's verify the structure of Deployment in creating pods.

screens.title: Deployment, ReplicaSet, Pod Template
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to switch templates, then follow the sequence of the deployment process that replaces pods.

visual.alt: This is a diagram showing how deployment alternately adjusts the scale of two ReplicaSets to replace pods.
labels: kubectl get deployments: READY / UP-TO-DATE / AVAILABLE

steps.title: Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, which in turn creates pods.
steps.body: Deployment is a resource that declares the desired state and enables the controller to adjust the actual state to match that desired state. Instead of creating pods directly, you create a ReplicaSet, which in turn creates pods behind the scenes. The ReplicaSet owned by a Deployment must not be managed directly.

steps.title: replicas and selector
steps.body: `spec.replicas` is the desired number of pods. `spec.selector` is a rule that finds which pods the ReplicaSet will manage based on labels, and it must match the labels of the pod template. To prevent unexpected conflicts with other controllers and selectors, this is ensured to not overlap.

steps.title: Changing the Pod template creates a new ReplicaSet.
steps.body: Modifying the pod template inside `spec.template` creates a new ReplicaSet. For example, changing the container image tag falls into this category. On the other hand, scaling by changing the number of replicas does not modify the template and therefore does not create a new ReplicaSet.

steps.title: The new grows, the old fades.
steps.body: Deployment gradually increases the size of a new ReplicaSet while gradually decreasing the size of the old ReplicaSet. This controlled pace of replacing pods is known as a rolling update. In the end, the new ReplicaSet holds only the desired number of pods, and the old ReplicaSet reaches zero.

steps.title: A new ReplicaSet increments its revision.
steps.body: When the Pod template changes, the Deployment revision increments with each rollout. Rollbacks also update the revision. This record allows reverting to a previous state based on the revision.

steps.title: Read progress status
steps.body: `kubectl get deployments`'s `READY` shows the number of ready replicas and the desired number, `UP-TO-DATE` shows the number updated with the latest template, and `AVAILABLE` shows the number available to users. Verify whether the rollout has completed using `kubectl rollout status deployment/name`.

screens.outro: Next, we examine the two values that determine the replacement rate.

screens.title: maxSurge·maxUnavailable and Rollback
screens.lead: Move the slider to observe how the range of available pod counts changes when replicas are set to 4, depending on the configuration.

visual.alt: Bar chart showing different lower and upper limits for pod counts during updates, depending on the configuration.

data.controlLabel: Setting maxUnavailable and maxSurge (based on replicas 4)

stops.body: The default values for `maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` are both 25%. Since maxUnavailable is rounded down and maxSurge is rounded up in percentage terms, when replicas are 4, maxUnavailable is 1 and maxSurge is 1. During an update, at least 3 pods must remain available, and the total number of pods can increase up to 5.

We first create a new pod instead of reducing an existing one. Only after the new pod is ready do we remove the old one, ensuring that the available pods are always four or more. The total number of pods is capped at five. Instead, one additional resource becomes necessary, and the replacement process proceeds slowly.

Create a new pod in the location where existing pods are reduced, without first adding a new pod. The replacement is fast and does not require additional resources, but it reduces the available pods to a minimum of two. For services where the new pod takes a long time to become ready, requests may easily fail.

`maxUnavailable` is 0, then `maxSurge` cannot also be 0, and vice versa. If both are 0, no pod can be scaled up or down, making it impossible to initiate a replacement. Although this combination appears safest, it is unusable.

`minReadySeconds` is the minimum time that a new pod must be in a ready state without container crashes, with a default value of 0. `progressDeadlineSeconds` is the time to wait before reporting progress as stalled, with a default of 600 seconds and must be greater than `minReadySeconds`. If the new version is unstable, it can be rolled back to the previous revision using `kubectl rollout undo deployment/name`, and a specific revision can be specified using `--to-revision`.

screens.outro: Let's apply these values to a service where model loading takes a long time.

screens.title: Explanation: Rolling update for a service where model loading takes a long time
screens.lead: The instructor configures deployment step by step for a service whose model takes tens of seconds to load. Select the right arrow to follow along.

visual.alt: Part of the Deployment Manifest containing the rolling update strategy and preparation time settings.

steps.title: Step 1: The pod does not immediately respond when it is spun up.
steps.body: After starting, this service's Pods take tens of seconds to load the model. During that time, the container is running but cannot answer requests. The key lesson is that creating a Pod does not immediately add usable capacity.

steps.title: Stage 2: It fails if traffic is present before the preparation signal.
steps.body: Traffic to the service fails when the new pod is not yet ready, but under the default settings, old pods may be terminated even before the new pod is ready, causing the service's capacity to drop temporarily.

steps.title: Step 3: Set maxUnavailable to 0.
steps.body: Do not reduce the old pod first; set `maxUnavailable` to near 0, here set to 0. Since the old pod is not deleted before the new pod is ready, the processing capacity does not drop below the desired level.

steps.title: Step 4: First scale up a new pod using maxSurge
steps.body: `maxUnavailable` If this is 0, then `maxSurge` must be greater than 0, so set it to 1. First, create an additional pod to load the model, and then reduce one of the old pods once it is ready. This process repeats until the replacement is complete. This approach requires temporarily additional resources equivalent to one pod.

steps.title: Step 5: Preparation Judgment Time and Congestion Detection
steps.body: `minReadySeconds` is set so that a new pod is considered ready and usable only after it maintains a ready state without any disruptions for a specified duration. For services whose model loading takes a long time, `progressDeadlineSeconds` is also set to a duration longer than the loading time, to prevent normal loading from being misinterpreted as a stall. If a stall persists for an extended period, it is reported using `ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.

steps.title: Step 6: Roll back if unstable
steps.body: If instability is observed in a new version, rollback to the previous revision using `kubectl rollout undo deployment/name`. Rolling back does not restart a few pods; instead, it initiates a new rollout using the template from the previous revision. Rolling back also updates the revision.

screens.outro: Finally, I will summarize the lecture content.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Before preparing, do not delete the old pod
screens.lead: We summarize the content of this class into three aspects: structure, speed, and recovery.

paragraphs: **Structure**: Deployment creates a ReplicaSet, which in turn creates Pods. When the Pod template changes, a new ReplicaSet and a new revision are created, and the new one gradually increases while the old one gradually decreases.

**Speed**: `maxSurge` is the limit on the number of pods that can be created beyond the desired number, while `maxUnavailable` is the limit on the number of pods that cannot be used during updates. The default value for both is 25%, and neither can be zero. To prevent removing old pods before new pods are ready, set `maxUnavailable` to a value close to zero and set `maxSurge` to a value greater than zero.
**Recovery**: Adjust judgment and identity detection using `minReadySeconds` and `progressDeadlineSeconds`; if unstable, revert to the previous revision using `kubectl rollout undo`.

checks.q: When rolling out an update for a service whose model takes tens of seconds to load, how should you configure it to add new Pods before removing old ones?
options: Set both maxSurge and maxUnavailable to 0.
Set maxUnavailable to a high value to quickly reduce old pods
Set maxUnavailable to something close to 0 and set maxSurge to something greater than 0.
Set maxSurge to 0 and extend only minReadySeconds.
checks.explain: Setting maxUnavailable close to zero allows you to first create and prepare new pods using maxSurge, and then scale down the old pods without immediately terminating the existing ones.

wrong.0: Both cannot be set to zero.
wrong.1: Setting maxUnavailable to a large value increases the window of service disruption due to newly created pods that are not yet ready.
wrong.3: If maxSurge is 0, there will be no headroom to scale up new pods before readiness, and old pods may be terminated during preparation.

glossary.def: This is a resource that declares the desired pod status and gradually replaces it through a ReplicaSet.
This is a method where pods are replaced at a controlled pace by scaling up a new ReplicaSet while scaling down the old ReplicaSet.
The maximum number of additional pods that can be created beyond the desired number of pods. The default is 25%.
The maximum number of pods that cannot be used during an update. The default is 25%.
This is an action that rolls back to the previous revision's pod template using kubectl rollout undo.

misconceptions.fact: If the criteria for determining when a new pod is ready to receive requests do not align with the replacement rate, failure intervals may occur.

misconceptions.myth: Setting both maxSurge and maxUnavailable to 0 is the safest option.
misconceptions.fact: Both cannot be zero. If one is zero, the other must be greater than zero for a replacement to proceed.

misconceptions.myth: Rollback involves restarting a few pods.
misconceptions.fact: Rollback is the action of initiating a new rollout using the pod template from a previous revision, and rollback also updates the Deployment's revision.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The old pod is not deleted before a new pod is ready.
maxSurge and maxUnavailable determine the replacement rate and availability.
Template changes create a new ReplicaSet and revision.
Rolls back to a previous revision if unstable.
